analysis.one_liner: Raises the salary cutoff for overtime pay and updates it automatically every year.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 20 Senate cosponsors including the majority leader, was referred to committee on March 29, 2023 and received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, salaried executive, administrative, and professional workers can be denied overtime pay only if they earn above a set salary threshold. That threshold sits at $35,568, so fewer than 15% of full-time salaried workers are guaranteed overtime today, down from 63% in 1975. The bill would raise the threshold in steps — $45,000, then $55,000, $65,000, and $75,000 by 2026 — and then tie it automatically each year to the 55th percentile of earnings for full-time salaried workers, which its findings estimate at roughly $82,745 by 2026. It would also narrow the duties test so that a worker who spends 20% or more of the time on non-managerial work cannot be classified as exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Salaried workers earning between roughly $35,568 and the new threshold — up to about $82,745 by 2026 — would become eligible for time-and-a-half pay for hours over 40. Workers reclassified as non-exempt would either be paid overtime or have hours capped. The bill's findings say this would restore overtime coverage to its historic range, and that when employers can no longer overwork exempt staff, they spread hours across the workforce, which also helps part-time workers who want full-time hours.

how_it_helps.text: Phases the overtime salary threshold from $45,000 to $75,000 by 2026, then to the 55th percentile of weekly earnings for full-time salaried workers, an inflation-adjusted projection of about $82,745 by 2026.
Updates the threshold automatically each year by law, ending the decades of drift that let coverage fall from 63% of salaried workers in 1975 to under 15% in 2022.
Tightens the duties test: the white-collar exemption no longer applies if at least 20% of a worker's duties are not directly or closely related to executive or administrative work.
Requires the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish quarterly data on weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers by region, making the automatic updates verifiable.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of salaried white-collar staff — retail and restaurant chains, banks, insurers, health systems, universities, and nonprofits — would pay overtime for staff now classified as exempt, or restructure jobs so staff work fewer hours. Some businesses would reclassify workers to hourly status or trim salaries to offset the new costs. Small employers with salaried managers near the threshold face the largest adjustment.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face materially higher labor costs for exempt salaried staff, and some would respond by converting salaried roles to hourly, capping hours, or trimming base pay, so not every affected worker ends up better paid.

The tightened 20% duties limit replaces a 40% retail-service standard with a stricter rule across the economy, and the boundary between exempt and non-exempt duties invites disputes and litigation over job classification.

A threshold near the 55th percentile of national earnings is a single national number; in low-wage regions it captures a much larger share of the salaried workforce than in high-wage regions, which some employers would argue is a blunt fit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: millions of salaried workers earning between roughly $36,000 and $83,000 would gain a right to time-and-a-half pay, and employers would bear the cost in wages or reduced hours. The automatic annual update is well designed — it prevents the threshold from silently decaying again, which is how coverage fell from 63% of salaried workers to under 15%. The main honest concerns are transition costs for small employers and classification disputes under the stricter duties test; those are real but secondary to the wage gain for workers.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on March 29, 2023 with 20 original cosponsors, including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren, and 17 other Democratic senators.

The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the standard first step — and the action record shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the Congress.

The bill would have raised the overtime salary threshold from the current $35,568 in steps to $75,000 by 2026, then tied it to the 55th percentile of full-time salaried weekly earnings, and tightened the duties test so the exemption fails if 20% or more of duties are non-managerial.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee; no chamber ever voted on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of salaried white-collar workers are better off: the $35,568 threshold and current duties rules stayed in place with no vote ever taken, and overtime coverage remains under 15% of full-time salaried workers. The senators who backed it, including its majority-leader cosponsor, never brought it to the floor.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Restoring Overtime Pay Act of 2023 with 20 cosponsors.

for.name: 19 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; it never came to the floor while the member who controls the Senate calendar was a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee (Chair Bernie Sanders, D-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 29, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.what_they_did: Offered no cosponsor; no Republican signed on at introduction, and the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Senate Democrats or the chamber's Independent; not one Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists to measure the split.

industries.industry: Retail, restaurant, and service chains with salaried managers
industries.note: Salaried store and restaurant managers are the classic exempt workforce; a threshold rising toward $83,000 would make them eligible for overtime or force hour caps, a direct cost to these employers.

industries.industry: Banks, insurers, and other salaried white-collar employers
industries.note: Professional and administrative staff earning between the current threshold and the new one would gain overtime rights, raising payroll costs or reshaping jobs.

industries.industry: Small businesses and nonprofits with salaried supervisors near the threshold
industries.note: The single national threshold covers a larger share of their salaried payrolls than in high-wage sectors, and reclassifying managers to hourly would hit them hardest, though affected staff would gain overtime rights.
